570     root-owned (the common case). Returns the destination path."""
571     golden = libvirt_golden_path(image)
572     print(f"==> installing verified qcow2 -> {golden} (libvirt golden)")
573     try:
574         os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(golden), exist_ok=True)
575         shutil.copyfile(srcq, golden)
576     except OSError:
```

The same module states that this pathname is an immutable backing store for every VM overlay at `scripts/deploy/xpf-deploy.py:594`:

```python
594     Each domain gets its OWN copy-on-write overlay instead
595     (`qemu-img create -f qcow2 -b <golden> -F qcow2 <overlay>`), so the
596     golden stays an immutable shared backing store and each VM writes
597     only to its distinct {name}.qcow2. A re-deploy re-creates the overlay
598     (a fresh boot from golden); `virt-install --name` still refuses to
599     redefine a live domain, so a running VM's overlay is not clobbered
600     out from under it.
```

- **Trace:** `fetch --install-libvirt` verifies a new qcow2, derives the default alias `xpf-appliance`, and calls `_install_libvirt_golden`. Existing VM disks were created with `-b /var/lib/libvirt/images/xpf-appliance.qcow2`. `copyfile` truncates/replaces those backing bytes in place; after a restart each overlay resolves the same path to a different base image, invalidating its cluster/data mapping. Both HA nodes commonly share that backing path.

- **Refutation attempt:** I checked preflight, deploy, destroy, and all six deploy test modules. They prove that each VM has a distinct writable overlay and that fetch/deploy agree on one path, but no code checks whether the golden is referenced, versions the backing filename, rebases overlays, or rejects an overwrite. Atomic replacement alone would not fix restart-time path resolution.

- **HPC/invariant check:** Not a dataplane hot-path issue. It violates qcow2 backing immutability, durable VM identity, and HA failure independence; a single management action can poison both nodes' disks.

- **Why it matters:** Installing a newer image under the default alias can corrupt or make unbootable every existing overlay, including both members of an HA pair. The next reboot can turn a routine image fetch into simultaneous appliance loss.

- **Fix direction:** Store verified goldens under immutable version/content-addressed filenames and have new overlays reference that exact path. Move only an alias/catalog pointer for future deployments. Refuse removal/replacement while libvirt overlays reference a base; provide an explicit, verified rebase/migration operation.

- **Labels:** deployment, libvirt, ha, data-integrity

- **Dedup note:** H-20/#4171/#4174 addressed two VMs attaching one writable golden; H-30/#4190 addressed fetch/deploy path drift. This finding is the new inverse failure created by overlays: mutating their supposedly immutable backing path.

- **Trace:** 1. A policy-permitted NAT64 first fragment allocates a translated source port and immediately publishes a global fragment-key -> decision entry. 2. The packet then fails a later commit condition, such as TTL/hop-limit expiry or `sessions.can_admit`, and is dropped. 3. `rollback_nat64_allocation` releases the port but has no fragment key and removes no association. 4. Delay publication to the cold first-fragment commit point; non-first lookup cost remains unchanged. If rollback deletion is used instead, carry a fixed-size pending key and remove it on every failure without allocating.

- **Fix direction:** Derive and hold a pending fragment key, then install only after session admission and successful forward-request construction/ownership transfer. The directly called map contract at `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/sharded_neighbor.rs:193` increments that single epoch for any existing key's MAC replacement:

```rust
193         // epoch so the worker fast path evicts those entries on their next
194         // hit. A FIRST insert (`prior_mac == None`) does NOT advance it:
195         // no cached flow can hold a stale MAC for a neighbor that did not

Every old flow now fails `neighbor_mac_epoch_stale` on its next packet, even when its own next-hop MAC is unchanged, and falls through to session/policy/neighbor resolution. 4. An on-link sender can repeatedly alternate the source/ARP MAC for one learnable IP, advancing the epoch faster than cache entries can remain warm. 5. Across workers, the flow cache becomes an expensive one-packet cache and policy/session slow-path load rises for all traffic.

- **Why it matters:** Small tunneled TCP/UDP packets can be deterministically emitted with invalid checksums, producing an interoperability/availability blackhole that depends on ingress frame padding rather than flow state.

- **Fix direction:** Make the IP-declared length authoritative whenever it is structurally valid and within the backing slice. Also harden `recompute_l4_checksum_ipv4/ipv6` to accept or derive an explicit declared upper-layer end. Add live-shaped `pkt_len=full Ethernet length` tests with v4 padding for GRE and WG and verify the decapsulated inner checksum.

- **Labels:** `correctness`, `checksum`, `ethernet-padding`, `tunnel`, `wireguard`, `gre`

- **Dedup note:** `#1641`/PR `#1655` fixed NAT64 reverse translation copying Ethernet padding into a newly translated IPv6 payload. This is a different root and path: same-family forward build performs a tunnel-forced full L4 recompute over slack, then GRE/WG removes the slack, invalidating the checksum. No `trim_l3_payload`, forced-recompute, or tunnel-padding match exists in the prior-report index.

### [A1-b3-F2] Every full filter evaluation allocates an empty `Arc` on the packet path

- **Title:** Every full filter evaluation allocates an empty `Arc` on the packet path

- **Severity:** Medium

- **Confidence:** High

- **Evidence:** `userspace-dp/src/filter/mod.rs:899`:
  ```rust
    fn default() -> Self {
        Self {
            action: FilterAction::Accept,
            dscp_rewrite: None,
            policer_name: String::new(),
            routing_instance: String::new(),
            forwarding_class: Arc::<str>::from(""),
            log: false,
            log_match: None,
  ```

- **Trace:** 1. A session miss or required full/cache-sensitive filter evaluation enters the shared evaluator. 2. The v4 and v6 loops initialize their accumulator with `FilterResult::default()`, including empty filters and misses. 3. `Arc::<str>::from("")` allocates an Arc control/data block even for an empty string. 4. The evaluator mutates or returns that result; when the result is released, Arc performs refcount/drop work and deallocates the block. 5. Repeated misses or cache-sensitive traffic repeat this allocator round trip per full evaluation.

- **Refutation attempt:** Checked whether empty `String` fields were the source (they are allocation-free), whether the value came from a shared static (it does not), and whether optimized Rust elides the Arc allocation. A standalone `rustc -O` counting-global-allocator probe using `black_box` reported `allocations=1` for exactly `Arc::<str>::from("")`. Cached TX-selection result types avoid this particular default, but the full enforcement evaluators call it at multiple v4/v6/lo0/interface entry points. Existing tests assert value equality, not allocation count.

- **HPC/invariant check:** This violates the campaign's zero-allocation warmed packet-path invariant. There is no unsafe provenance or aliasing problem, but allocation/deallocation and Arc's atomic release add variable latency, allocator contention, and cache traffic. The behavior remains in optimized release code as confirmed by the `-O` probe.

- **Why it matters:** Filter evaluation is attacker-driveable on new flows and cache-sensitive packets. One unconditional heap allocation per evaluation reduces throughput and worsens tail latency under exactly the traffic patterns where firewall enforcement is busiest.

- **Fix direction:** Represent the absent forwarding class without ownership, preferably `Option<Arc<str>>` with `None` as the default and allocation/clone only when a term sets a class. Preserve the external empty-string behavior at a cold boundary if required. Add an allocator-count regression test or benchmark for empty, miss, accept and discard evaluations in release mode.

- **Labels:** performance, hpc, firewall-filter, allocation, policy-filter-screen

- **Dedup note:** Aggressive searches found no prior `FilterResult`/empty-Arc report. `#919` concerns cloning `Arc<str>` in session metadata, a different object, call path, and root cause; this finding is unconditional construction of a new empty Arc by the filter result default.

The wide O(N) route scan and Vec allocation are cold but add activation latency.

- **Labels:** session-ha, split-rg, stale-state, resource-lifetime

- **Title:** Poisoned shared-session reads bypass install/delete generation guards

- **Severity:** Medium

~~~rust

            .lock()
            .ok()
            .and_then(|sessions| sessions.get(&entry.key).cloned());
        // #2170 install-side guard (SMR C3): refuse a strictly-older-
        // generation install so the per-key stored generation never
        // regresses (closes the delayed-stale-install variant on the
        // helper). Only acts when BOTH the stored and incoming generations
        // are non-zero — local-origin entries (generation 0) and legacy
~~~

The guard consequently does not run at userspace-dp/src/afxdp/ha.rs:291-297:

~~~rust

            && previous.generation != 0
            && entry.generation != 0
            && entry.generation < previous.generation
        {
            SESSION_INSTALL_STALE_IGNORED.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
            return;
~~~

The subsequent mutation uses recovery rather than failing, at userspace-dp/src/afxdp/shared_ops.rs:31-40:

~~~rust
pub(super) fn lock_shared_recover<T>(m: &Mutex<T>) -> MutexGuard<'_, T> {
    match m.lock() {
        Ok(guard) => guard,
        Err(poisoned) => {
            m.clear_poison();
            SHARED_SESSION_POISON_RECOVERIES.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
            eprintln!(
                "xpf-ha: shared session mutex poisoned by a prior worker panic; recovering existing sessions and clearing poison"
            );
            poisoned.into_inner()
~~~

delete_synced_session_gen repeats the same .lock().ok() pattern at userspace-dp/src/afxdp/ha.rs:437-449, and purge_remapped_tunnel_sessions returns zero on poison at lines 532-541.

- **Trace:** 1. Generation 2 for key K is committed in the shared map. 2. A contained worker panic while holding that mutex poisons it; the committed map remains available through PoisonError::into_inner. 3. A delayed generation-1 upsert reaches Coordinator. 4. lock().ok() returns None, so the install-side comparison sees no existing generation and accepts generation 1. 5. publish_shared_session immediately locks the same mutex through lock_shared_recover, clears poison, and replaces generation 2 with generation 1; stale worker commands are broadcast. The delete variant similarly bypasses its comparison and then recovers/removes the newer entry.

- **Refutation attempt:** Inspected the lock recovery helper, generation types/tests, Coordinator callers, worker upsert behavior, and the Go delete guard. The authoritative Go guard prevents normal stale cluster deletes from reaching the helper, but the Rust method explicitly supports future/non-Go generation-aware deletes and stale installs have no equivalent downstream guard. Existing tests independently validate poison recovery and generation ordering; none combines them. Recovery after the check proves poison is not a fail-stop that would prevent mutation.

- **HPC/invariant check:** This is safe Rust with no aliasing or FFI issue. Mutex poison is exceptional/cold; Relaxed metrics are adequate. The invariant failure is control-state monotonicity: validation and mutation apply conflicting poison policies to the same protected map. No packet bounds, byte order, UMEM, or cache-line concern changes the result.

- **Why it matters:** After a contained panic, delayed HA traffic can roll a key backward or delete its newer replacement, recreating the stale-install/delete hazards generation guards were added to prevent. That can remove valid standby state or install obsolete NAT/forwarding policy for takeover.

- **Fix direction:** Use lock_shared_recover for every shared-session read that participates in correctness, including generation checks and tunnel purge. Prefer validating and committing the canonical map entry under one recovered critical section, then derive aliases/indexes and worker commands from the accepted result. Add poison-plus-stale-upsert and poison-plus-stale-delete tests.

- **Labels:** session-ha, concurrency, generation-ordering, fail-closed

- **Dedup note:** #2402 fixed poison-as-empty specifically in activation prewarm, while #2170/#2221 added generation ordering. This is their materially different composition at Coordinator ingress: the guard reads with nonrecovering .ok(), then the write recovers and proceeds. Neither closed issue covers this call-site/invariant failure.

Each unique key scans the entire growing result at userspace-dp/src/afxdp/session_glue/commands/demote_owner_rgs.rs:94-101:

                &publish_metadata,
                origin,

### [A1-b5-F1] Extend shared non-exact lease conservation through initialization and teardown

- **Title:** Extend shared non-exact lease conservation through initialization and teardown

- **Severity:** Medium

- **Confidence:** High

- **Evidence:** `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/cos/builders.rs:203` gives every shaped non-exact worker replica a full private buffer before any shared lease acquisition:

  ```rust
  203                     tokens: if queue.transmit_rate_bytes == 0 {
  204                         queue.buffer_bytes.max(COS_MIN_BURST_BYTES)
  205                     } else if queue.exact {
  206                         0
  207                     } else {
  208                         queue.buffer_bytes.max(COS_MIN_BURST_BYTES)
  209                     },
  ```

  `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/cos/queue_service/mod.rs:1384` confirms that these same non-exact queues are now supposed to be class-wide lease-metered:

  ```rust
  1384         // #4265 (R-2): meter the guarantee refill through the shared queue
  1385         // lease when the coordinator attached one (a sharded non-exact
  1386         // guaranteed queue, rate >= COS_SHARED_EXACT_MIN_RATE_BYTES). All
  1387         // workers draw from the one legacy lease -> aggregate admission ==
  1388         // configured rate. When no lease is attached (single-owner low-rate
  1389         // non-exact queue), `maybe_top_up_cos_queue_lease` falls through to
  1390         // the same per-worker `refill_cos_tokens` used before this change,
  1391         // so single-owner behaviour is unchanged. The legacy lease returns
  ```

  `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/cos/token_bucket.rs:426` then excludes every non-exact queue from teardown give-back:

  ```rust
  426         .flat_map(|(&root_ifindex, root)| {
  427             root.queues
  428                 .iter()
  429                 .enumerate()
  430                 .filter(|(_, queue)| queue.config.exact && queue.hot.tokens > 0)
  431                 .map(move |(queue_idx, _)| (root_ifindex, queue_idx))
  432         })
  433         .collect::<Vec<_>>();
  ```

  The directly called worker-exit contract invokes that filtered release immediately before the worker terminates (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/worker/loop_body/mod.rs:1297`):

  ```rust
  1297     for binding in bindings.iter_mut() {
  1298         clear_all_cos_exact_backlogs_for_binding(binding);
  1299         release_all_cos_root_leases(binding);
  1300         release_all_cos_queue_leases(binding);
  1301     }
  ```

- **Trace:** 1. The coordinator attaches one legacy `SharedCoSQueueLease` to a sharded non-exact guaranteed class. 2. A worker lazily builds its runtime; `builders.rs` exposes `buffer_bytes` of local tokens without acquiring them, and every peer does the same. 3. `maybe_top_up_cos_queue_lease` returns early while those tokens exceed its watermark, so shared `outstanding_leased_tokens` remains zero. 4. Guarantee sends debit the local tokens and call `lease.consume`; its saturating outstanding subtraction cannot charge credit that was never acquired. The class can therefore emit approximately `N_workers * buffer_bytes` of cold-start/rebuild burst outside its class lease, although the root lease still caps whole-interface traffic. 5. Independently, if a non-exact worker has legitimately leased but unused tokens when a runtime reset or worker exit occurs, `release_all_cos_queue_leases` skips it because `exact == false`; the queue is dropped but outstanding credit remains charged in the reused shared lease. Repeated active resets/exits can consume the outstanding headroom and suppress the class until the lease object is rebuilt.

- **Refutation attempt:** Exact queues are safe at construction because they start at zero, but that branch does not cover the newly leased non-exact queues. The shared root lease was inspected and only bounds aggregate interface bytes; it cannot restore per-class guarantee fairness. Normal empty-queue settlement in `tx_completion.rs:759-810` does return any attached queue lease, but reset/exit explicitly supports nonempty queues and calls the filtered teardown helper before clearing/dropping them. The `#4265` aggregate test does not refute startup over-credit: it leaves six 256 KiB initial buckets intact and accepts anything below three times a 20 ms expected budget. No assigned test exercises non-exact teardown.

- **HPC/invariant check:** For a class-wide lease, every byte visible in any worker's `queue.hot.tokens` must have a matching shared outstanding charge, and `available + outstanding` plus no untracked local credit must stay within the configured burst. Destruction/replacement must return all unused outstanding credit exactly once. Both halves are violated. The fix must remain cold-path for initialization/teardown and preserve the allocation-free CAS-only warmed acquire path.

- **Why it matters:** Cold start/config rebuild can transiently let a non-exact class take more than its configured guarantee share from exact peers; active worker resets can do the opposite and progressively under-serve or stall that guaranteed class. This is fail-open for class fairness on initialization and fail-closed for availability on teardown, while firewall packet-policy enforcement itself is unchanged.

- **Fix direction:** Make lease presence part of runtime token initialization: initialize a shaped non-exact queue at zero when its fast path has a shared lease, or immediately reconcile the builder's tokens through an acquire before exposing the queue. Generalize teardown enumeration to every queue with an attached shared lease, not `config.exact`, and return via `release_unused_v8` (which already reduces to legacy give-back). Add short-window `N`-worker conservation, runtime reset, lease-map replacement, and worker-exit tests.

- **Labels:** `cos`, `scheduler-fairness`, `lease-accounting`, `lifecycle`

- **Dedup note:** `#4265` fixed recurring private full-rate refill in selection; this is the constructor/reset/exit lifecycle left outside that patch. `#4246` fixed exact/v8 epoch-ledger give-back; this finding is the non-exact legacy queue excluded by the exact-only caller filter. Searches for `nonexact startup`, `queue lease teardown`, `outstanding worker exit`, the cited symbols, and both paths found no prior indexed finding with this root cause.

  97     let mut dropped_mirror_reserve = false;
  98     while binding.scratch.scratch_local_tx.len() < batch_size {
  99         let Some(mut req) = pending.pop_front() else {
  100             break;
  101         };

- **Trace:** 1. A Local CoS batch contains mirror flow A first and ordinary flow B second while the free-frame count is at the mirror reserve. 2. `submit_local` records sidecar entries `[A, B]`. 3. `transmit_batch` pops and drops A, then stages and transmits B; it returns `(packets=1, bytes=len(B))`. 4. `submit_local` applies `sidecar[..1]`, charging B's transmission bytes to A's flow bucket, and applies the same numeric-prefix assumption to enqueue timestamps. 5. Prepared submission preserves a true prefix and does not refute the Local path. The Local return type contains only counts/bytes, not committed identities, so the caller cannot reconstruct the filtered sequence. Assigned mirror tests drop before sidecar creation or use `mirror_clone=false` in end-to-end submit/sojourn tests. The file header itself acknowledges this exact carry-over defect.

- **HPC/invariant check:** Per-flow rate and sojourn feedback must be identity-preserving: every committed descriptor contributes once to the bucket/timestamp belonging to that descriptor, independent of admission filtering. A count-only commit token is insufficient after non-prefix filtering. The repair should keep fixed stack storage and avoid allocation/dynamic dispatch.

- **Why it matters:** Under frame pressure, mirror traffic can poison the feedback used by flow-cap fairness and misstate queue latency. The data packet still follows the correct firewall verdict, but scheduler fairness decisions become based on another flow's service history.

- **Fix direction:** Have `transmit_batch` fill a caller-provided fixed-size committed-index/metadata array, move bucket/enqueue metadata alongside each staged request, or perform mirror-reserve filtering before sidecar construction. Account the exact committed identities and add front/interior mirror-drop tests with distinct flow buckets and enqueue timestamps.

- **Labels:** `cos`, `scheduler-fairness`, `mirror`, `accounting`

- **Dedup note:** The source marks this as a tracked carry-over, but the supplied dedup index has no matching issue, PR, or prior finding under `sidecar`, `mirror prefix`, `submit_local`, `sojourn`, or `transmit_batch`. Reported as known-but-unindexed, not as a newly introduced regression.

- **Title:** Fail closed when fairness evidence is incomplete per stream or scrape series

- **Severity:** Medium

- **Confidence:** High

- **Evidence:** `userspace-dp/src/fairness_eval/windowing.rs:89` appends only stream records present in an accepted interval:

  ```rust
  89         for s in &interval.streams {
  90             let bytes = (s.bits_per_second / 8.0) as u64;
  91             per_stream_buckets.entry(s.socket).or_default().push(bytes);
  92         }
  93         aggregate_buckets_bps.push(iv_total_bps as u64);

  The overall coverage gate at `userspace-dp/src/fairness_eval/windowing.rs:101` counts intervals, not cells for every connected stream:

  ```rust
  101     let observed_buckets = aggregate_buckets_bps.len() as u64;
  102     if observed_buckets + STEADY_STATE_SAMPLE_SLACK_SECS < MIN_STEADY_STATE_SECS {
  103         return Err(format!(
  104             "observed {observed_buckets} in-window 1s buckets < {MIN_STEADY_STATE_SECS}s minimum \
  105              (declared duration {total_dur}s, but the iperf JSON carries too few non-omitted \
  106              intervals — truncated or heavily-omitted run); a meaningful CoV needs a full \
  107              steady-state window"
  108         ));
  ```

  Means then divide by the number of present cells (`userspace-dp/src/fairness_eval/windowing.rs:111`):

  ```rust
  111     // Per-stream window-mean throughput for the per-flow CoV input.
  112     let per_flow_throughputs: Vec<u64> = per_stream_buckets
  113         .values()
  114         .filter(|v| !v.is_empty())
  115         .map(|v| {
  116             let sum: u64 = v.iter().sum();
  117             sum / v.len() as u64
  118         })
  119         .collect();
  ```

  The scrape reducer deliberately creates its timestamp universe only from surviving rows (`userspace-dp/src/fairness_eval/per_worker.rs:141`):

  ```rust
  141 /// Missing whole scrapes (a Prometheus scrape gap where NO worker on the
  142 /// source emitted) do not appear in the universe, so a scrape gap is not
  143 /// fabricated into spurious zeros.
  144 fn median_per_worker_zero_filled(
  145     per_ts_worker: &BTreeMap<(u64, u32), u32>,
  146     n_total_workers: u32,
  147 ) -> Vec<u32> {
  148     let timestamps: std::collections::BTreeSet<u64> =
  149         per_ts_worker.keys().map(|(ts, _)| *ts).collect();
  ```

- **Trace:** 1. `start.connected` declares flows A and B and the JSON has 60 accepted intervals, so the overall coverage gate passes. 2. A appears in every interval; B appears once at a healthy rate and is absent from the other 59 due to a partial/truncated stream series. 3. B's vector is nonempty, so it is neither zero-filled nor dropped; its mean divides by one and can equal A's mean, yielding observed CoV 0 even though B delivered about 1/60 of A over the window. 4. A sparse binding/CoS TSV containing one balanced in-window scrape is also accepted because there is no minimum timestamp count; the sum and RSS guards can pass. 5. Another flow can keep aggregate throughput at the structural cap, so even `--expect-saturation` need not catch the missing B evidence, and the reducer can emit `PASS` on an unauditable/unfair run.

- **Refutation attempt:** Seeding from `start.connected` catches a stream absent for the entire window, but any one present sample defeats that protection. `#4277`'s 60-bucket check validates only aggregate interval count. `median_per_worker_zero_filled` catches a worker missing at timestamps where another matching worker emitted, but explicitly omits whole scrape gaps and has no sample-density threshold. The assigned tests cover omitted intervals, globally truncated interval sets, and dead workers across existing timestamps; none covers partial stream cardinality or a one-scrape fairness series.

- **HPC/invariant check:** A merge-gating fairness reducer must prove evidence completeness before computing a verdict: every connected stream needs one value (or an explicit zero) for every accepted interval, and binding/CoS telemetry needs a minimum/density-bounded timestamp series over the same window. Missing evidence must produce an error, not a favorable statistic. This is offline tooling, so stricter validation has no dataplane latency cost.

- **Why it matters:** The evaluator is the acceptance gate for scheduler fairness work. Treating missing cells as non-events can certify a flow with near-total outage and a structurally sparse scrape as fair, undermining the evidence used to merge or qualify CoS changes.

- **Fix direction:** Build each accepted interval against the seeded connected-socket set; reject duplicate/unknown sockets and either zero-fill or fail on missing sockets according to an explicit contract. Require binding and selected-CoS scrape coverage close to the steady-state duration with bounded gaps, and report counts/gaps. Add end-to-end false-PASS regressions for one-of-60 stream samples and one balanced scrape.

- **Labels:** `fairness-eval`, `validation`, `fail-open`, `test-gap`

### [A1-b6-F1] Post-NAT wire keys are reused to re-evaluate pre-NAT ingress TX-selection policy

- **Severity:** Medium

- **Confidence:** High

- **Evidence:** `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx/cos_classify.rs:607-615` re-walks the ingress input filter using the single `flow_key` supplied for output TX selection:

  ```rust
  let ingress_result = if let Some(now_ns) = now_ns {
      crate::filter::evaluate_filter_ref_tx_selection_runtime_uncounted(
          ingress_filter,
          flow_key.src_ip,
          flow_key.dst_ip,
          flow_key.protocol,
          flow_key.src_port,
          flow_key.dst_port,
          meta.dscp,
  ```

  The cached branch repeats the same tuple use at `cos_classify.rs:250-258`. Direct callers establish the mismatch: `afxdp/forward_request.rs:180-194,207-218` derives and passes `forward_wire_key` specifically for post-NAT output matching, while `afxdp/flow_cache.rs:454-467` does the same when constructing a cached descriptor.

- **Trace:** 1. A pre-NAT ingress input-filter term matches the private client tuple and assigns `forwarding-class`, DSCP rewrite, or a three-color policer. 2. The normal input action evaluation sees the original ingress tuple. 3. SNAT/DNAT produces a different wire address and possibly port. 4. `build_live_forward_request_from_frame` or flow-cache installation passes only that post-NAT wire key to the CoS resolver so the output filter gets correct Junos ordering. 5. The resolver reuses it for the ingress filter rewalk. 6. The authored ingress term no longer matches, so its queue/rewrite is lost and its three-color policer is not metered; terminal input action remains separately enforced.

- **Refutation attempt:** Inspected both live and cached callers, ingress logical-ifindex selection, filter action evaluation, TX-selection evaluator variants, count deduplication, and tests. The action path prevents a terminal security verdict bypass, but it does not carry the matched ingress modifiers or policer result into TX selection. Existing `#3642` tests prove post-NAT output matching only; ingress tests keep the tuple unchanged. The defect therefore survives with reduced scope: CoS classification/remarking and ingress three-color policing, not terminal input allow/deny.

- **HPC/invariant check:** The fix should preserve the current allocation-free single filter walk per stage. Carry distinct pre-NAT ingress and post-NAT output keys (or the already evaluated ingress modifiers) without cloning heap-backed keys on the packet path.

- **Why it matters:** NAT can silently move traffic out of its configured queue, omit ingress DSCP rewrite, or bypass an ingress rate-control drop. This diverges from vSRX/Junos stage ordering and can turn a configured policer into a no-op for translated traffic.

- **Fix direction:** Split the resolver contract into `ingress_key` and `egress_wire_key`, using the former only for the input-filter rewalk and the latter only for output filtering. Update live and cache-install callers and add SNAT/DNAT forward/reverse tests for forwarding-class, DSCP rewrite, and three-color drop.

- **Labels:** `userspace-dp`, `afxdp`, `cos`, `nat`, `firewall-filter`, `tx-umem-xsk`, `vsrx-parity`

- **Dedup note:** `#3642`/PR `#3648` fixed the opposite stage: output filters previously saw the pre-NAT tuple. This is a residual caused by feeding that corrected post-NAT key back into the ingress stage; it has a different root and affected policy surface.

### [A1-b6-F3] A 1280-byte floor bypasses TCP segmentation for valid smaller IPv4 interface MTUs

- **Title:** A 1280-byte floor bypasses TCP segmentation for valid smaller IPv4 interface MTUs

- **Severity:** Medium

- **Confidence:** High

- **Evidence:** The dispatch admission predicate floors all plain-interface MTUs in `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx/dispatch/mod.rs:1449-1455`:

  ```rust
  let mtu = forwarding
      .egress
      .get(&decision.resolution.egress_ifindex)
      .or_else(|| forwarding.egress.get(&decision.resolution.tx_ifindex))
      .map(|egress| egress.mtu)
      .unwrap_or_default()
      .max(1280);
  ```

  The prepared segment builder independently repeats it at `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx/tcp_segmentation.rs:24-30`:

  ```rust
  let mtu = forwarding
      .egress
      .get(&decision.resolution.egress_ifindex)
      .or_else(|| forwarding.egress.get(&decision.resolution.tx_ifindex))
      .map(|egress| egress.mtu)
      .unwrap_or_default()
      .max(1280);
  ```

- **Trace:** 1. A valid IPv4 egress is configured with MTU 576 or 900; snapshot validation accepts any nonnegative `i32` and preserves it. 2. A non-DF TCP IPv4 datagram has L3 length above that MTU but below 1280. 3. `forwarded_tcp_may_need_segmentation` compares against 1280 and returns false. 4. The raw-MTU PTB helper sees the oversize packet but correctly returns `Forward` for IPv4 `DF=0`. 5. Normal dispatch submits an L3 packet larger than the configured egress MTU to AF_XDP TX. 6. The driver/device must reject, drop, or emit an interface-MTU-violating packet; the dataplane neither segments nor reports a segmentation miss.

- **Refutation attempt:** Inspected interface MTU validation, the duplicate frame-copy segmenter, dispatch ordering, the raw-MTU PTB decision, DF semantics, and all assigned segmentation/PTB tests. The 1280 minimum is valid for IPv6 links, but it is not an IPv4 minimum; `forwarded_egress_mtu_decision` itself uses the IPv4 floor 68. DF-set traffic gets PTB and masks this path, but non-DF traffic does not. No validator enforces MTU >=1280 and no assigned test uses a smaller IPv4 MTU.

- **HPC/invariant check:** Removing the floor adds no hot-path work. Keep one resolved actual MTU, preserve `0` as unknown, and perform any IPv6-specific minimum validation outside the per-packet segmenter.

- **Why it matters:** Low-MTU IPv4 links can blackhole ordinary non-DF TCP traffic in the exact size interval `(configured_mtu, 1280]`. The silent path also bypasses the segmentation-miss telemetry operators would use to diagnose it.

- **Fix direction:** Use the actual nonzero egress MTU in both the predicate and both segmentation builders. Treat MTU 0 as unknown consistently. Add IPv4 MTU 576/900 tests for DF and non-DF frames, plus MTU 0 and IPv6 minimum-policy tests.

- **Labels:** `userspace-dp`, `afxdp`, `tcp`, `mtu`, `xsk-tx`, `tx-umem-xsk`, `vsrx-parity`

- **Dedup note:** `ps-review-038 A1-R2` is the separate large-MTU-to-`u16` truncation in segment length fields. This finding concerns small valid IPv4 MTUs being raised before admission/build and has a different trigger and root cause.

Earlier peer A has no active attempt, so its `drive_attempt_machine` swaps the single engine `handshake_request_pending` flag to false. 4. - **Trace:** 1. Old monitor M1 blocks in `recv` or its initial dump. 2.    24 /// WireGuard reject-after-messages limit.
   25 ///
   26 /// Per the protocol, a session must stop encrypting after this many
   27 /// transport messages and rekey.

  ```

  ```rust

  293             // (which post-init is always already-seen because we
  294             // marked bit 0 on accept) or a strictly older counter.
  295             let age = self.highest - c;
  296             if age >= REPLAY_WINDOW {
  297                 ReplayDecision::OutOfWindow
  298             } else {
  299                 let mask = 1u64 << age;
  300                 if self.bitmap & mask != 0 {
  ```

  The boundary is intentional in `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/wg/session.rs:384-392`:

  ```rust
  384         let mut r = ReplayState::default();
  385         assert_eq!(r.check_and_update(0), ReplayDecision::Accept);
  386         // Move the window so 0 is at the trailing edge but still
  387         // in-window: highest = 63, age = 63 < 64.
  388         assert_eq!(r.check_and_update(63), ReplayDecision::Accept);
  389         assert_eq!(r.check_and_update(0), ReplayDecision::Repeat);
  390         // One more step pushes 0 out: highest = 64, age = 64 = REPLAY_WINDOW.
  391         assert_eq!(r.check_and_update(64), ReplayDecision::Accept);
  392         assert_eq!(r.check_and_update(0), ReplayDecision::OutOfWindow);
  ```

  In contrast, the official [wireguard-go replay filter](https://git.zx2c4.com/wireguard-go/commit/?id=22af3890f60d11472977f2fbdf50e6d5b406e356) uses 128 64-bit ring blocks and an 8,128-counter backtrack window; WireGuard Linux uses the same class of fixed replay bitmap in its [receive path](https://git.zx2c4.com/wireguard-linux/tree/drivers/net/wireguard/receive.c).

- **Trace:** 1. Counter C is delayed in a queue or on one path while authenticated records C+1 through C+64 reach xpf first. 2. Each newer record decrypts and advances the highest counter; C has never been accepted and is not a replay. 3. C later passes header/session/counter-ceiling checks and AEAD authentication. 4. The post-AEAD replay update computes `age = 64` and returns `OutOfWindow`. 5. The engine zeroes the authentic plaintext and drops it; reference WG peers retain roughly two orders of magnitude more reorder depth.

- **Refutation attempt:** The replay state is mutex-protected, update occurs only after successful AEAD, and duplicate bits are correct within the chosen width. The precheck and post-AEAD update both use the same 64 constant, so this is not merely a cheap prefilter followed by a wider authoritative window. Tests explicitly enforce the 64 boundary. A narrower window does not permit replay and therefore is not a confidentiality/authentication break, but concurrency safety does not prevent false rejection of unseen authentic packets. The availability/interoperability claim survived.

- **HPC/invariant check:** Preserve zero-allocation, post-AEAD update, and O(1) normal work. A reference-shaped `[u64; 128]` ring adds 1 KiB per live session; a normal packet touches metadata plus one bitmap word, while a large jump clears at most 128 words. Benchmark session cache footprint and the existing replay mutex, but do not trade correctness for a single-word bitmap.

- **Why it matters:** At high packet rates, 64 packets can represent only tens of microseconds. Multi-queue scheduling, path diversity, failover, or transient queueing can exceed that depth, causing bursts of valid inner packets to be discarded and producing TCP retransmission/throughput collapse that a kernel or wireguard-go peer would not exhibit.

- **Fix direction:** Adopt the reference 8,128-counter ring-window algorithm or a proven WireGuard replay implementation. Keep the current precheck as a non-mutating optimization only if it uses the same authoritative width. Add unseen-counter tests at ages 64, 127, 8,127, and 8,128 plus a large-jump ring-clear test and a release benchmark.

- **Trace:** 1. The daemon detects pending RETH MAC programming, sets DeferWorkers, and sends a changed-plan snapshot. 2. Policy-only preflight passes, but a non-policy field is invalid (for example interface address, CoS queue, NAT64/NPTv6 rule) or a mandatory map pin cannot be opened; those checks live in the full forwarding/reconcile build. 3. The handler prunes tunnel control resources, stores/replans the incoming snapshot, skips reconcile because defer_workers is true, refreshes status, sets persist_state, and replies ok=true. 4a. If MAC programming does not require a link cycle, the daemon clears defer and reapplies; the full build now rejects, but the caller logs only a warning, leaving old workers/forwarding active while the newly persisted desired snapshot/status has already been accepted. 4b. If a link cycle occurred, workers were stopped; rebind attempts the full build, discards its error, refreshes/persists again, and can leave no forwarding workers. 5. Restart reads the invalid accepted snapshot as the boot baseline, extending the failure.

The invariant is: ok=true and persisted desired/applied generation must mean the snapshot is fully buildable with mandatory resources, even when activation is intentionally deferred; no side-effecting prune may precede acceptance. Unsafe/UMEM ownership is not directly violated because worker teardown/join is elsewhere, but desired/applied/debt state is conflated.

- **Why it matters:** An invalid snapshot can be acknowledged and made durable without ever being runnable. Depending on link-cycle path, enforcement remains silently on old policy (fail-open relative to the accepted desired config) or workers remain stopped (availability failure), while status/persistence imply success.

- **Fix direction:** Add a side-effect-free full forwarding and mandatory-map preflight before tunnel pruning or stored/status mutation in the defer branch. On failure, return ok=false with the prior snapshot, status, threads, and persistence untouched. If staging is intentional, model staged desired separately from applied state/debt, make response semantics explicit, and have rebind propagate activation failure. Add both link-cycle and no-link-cycle tests for each non-policy integrity class and missing map pins.

### [A1-b10-F3] Slowpath never demotes io_uring after a permanent runtime write failure

- **Title:** Slowpath never demotes io_uring after a permanent runtime write failure

- **Severity:** Medium

- **Confidence:** High

- **Evidence:** The mode is selected only at initialization. userspace-dp/src/slowpath.rs:421-430:

~~~rust
    let mut mode = match IoUring::new(256) {
        Ok(ring) => {
            status.set_mode("io_uring");
            WriteMode::IoUring(ring)
        }
        Err(err) => {
            status.set_mode("sync");
            status.set_last_error(format!("slow-path io_uring unavailable: {err}"));
            WriteMode::SyncFallback
        }
~~~

Every later packet continues to dispatch according to that unchanged mode. userspace-dp/src/slowpath.rs:433-440:

~~~rust
    while let Ok(req) = rx.recv() {
        status.queued_packets.fetch_sub(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
        let result = match &mut mode {
            WriteMode::IoUring(ring) => {
                write_packet_io_uring_or_sync(ring, tun.as_raw_fd(), &req.bytes)
            }
            WriteMode::SyncFallback => write_packet_sync(tun.as_raw_fd(), &req.bytes),
        };
~~~

Errors update counters/text but not mode. userspace-dp/src/slowpath.rs:448-455:

~~~rust
            Err(err) => {
                status.write_errors.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
                status.dropped_packets.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
                status
                    .dropped_bytes
                    .fetch_add(req.bytes.len() as u64, Ordering::Relaxed);
                status.set_last_error(err);
            }
~~~

Only failures classified as definitely transferring nothing receive a one-call synchronous retry; ambiguous/partial errors are dropped. userspace-dp/src/slowpath.rs:675-681:

~~~rust
    match result {
        Ok(()) => Ok(()),
        Err(err) if err.safe_to_retry() => sync_fallback(),
        // Bytes are (or may be) already on the TUN — re-sending would
        // double-transmit / corrupt the device. Drop the packet (the caller
        // counts it as a write error + drop).
        Err(err) => Err(err.to_string()),
~~~

The sibling state writer proves runtime demotion is not automatic in io_uring_write. userspace-dp/src/state_writer.rs:343-349:

~~~rust
    if outcome.io_uring_failed && matches!(mode, WriteMode::IoUring(_)) {
        *mode = WriteMode::SyncFallback;
        active.store(false, Ordering::Relaxed);
        if let Ok(mut m) = mode_str.lock() {
            *m = "sync".to_string();
        }
    }
~~~

- **Trace:** 1. Slowpath starts successfully in io_uring mode. 2. A later ring/kernel/fd condition causes a permanent submission/wait/completion failure. 3a. If the helper classifies the failure as NothingWritten, that one packet may succeed through synchronous fallback, but mode/status remain io_uring and the next packet retries the broken ring. 3b. If the result is Transferred or ambiguous, retry is correctly forbidden to prevent duplicate TUN frames, so the packet is counted as dropped; mode still remains io_uring. 4. Every subsequent locally originated or reinjected control packet repeats the failure path, allocation/error formatting, and possibly loss, with no transition to the usable synchronous transport.

- **Refutation attempt:** io_uring_write retries EINTR and drains/matches stale completions, so common transient errors do not necessarily reach this caller. It also correctly prevents whole-frame resend after a possible partial transfer. Neither behavior repairs a ring that has become permanently unusable. The state_writer contains explicit caller-owned demotion, confirming the shared helper does not mutate mode. slowpath tests cover decide_sync_fallback for a single call but never send a second packet or assert status/mode transition. #2478 fixed a bounded helper spin, not persistent caller mode; #2958 fixed this pattern only in state_writer. Immediate ring destruction must also respect #2297 outstanding-SQE lifetime, but that makes the fix careful rather than refuting the repeated-failure state. The claim survives.

- **HPC/invariant check:** Slowpath is off the AF_XDP forwarding hot loop, but it carries routing/control and local traffic. The invariant is: after a transport-level runtime ring failure, safely retire/cancel/reap ring ownership once, publish degraded sync mode, and never repeatedly submit to a known-bad ring. Relaxed telemetry ordering is sufficient and not the cause. Any demotion must first prove no SQE still references packet memory.

- **Why it matters:** A one-time ring failure can turn into sustained packet loss for BGP/OSPF/management/local traffic, or at minimum impose one failed ring operation and error-string update on every packet despite a working synchronous fallback.

- **Fix direction:** Return a structured outcome separating packet transfer certainty from ring health. After a terminal ring-health failure, safely cancel/reap or otherwise retain all referenced buffers until CQE ownership is resolved, then replace mode with SyncFallback and update status once. Preserve no-retry semantics for the current ambiguous/partial packet. Test two consecutive packets for permanent NothingWritten and ambiguous failures, including mode/status/counter assertions.

- **Labels:** bug, slowpath, availability, performance, io_uring

- **Dedup note:** #2958 reported and fixed runtime demotion for state_writer; slowpath has a separate mode loop and remains unchanged. #2478 covered helper retry spinning, and #2297/#2312 cover outstanding SQE/CQE lifetime. This finding is the distinct packet-loss/repeated-failure caller state, with Medium severity because it affects slowpath control traffic.

        binding = USERSPACE_BINDINGS.get(fallback_idx);
    }
  ```

  ```rust
    let queue_count = candidates.iter().map(|(_, rx)| *rx).min().unwrap_or(0);
    let interfaces = candidates
        .iter()
        .map(|(name, _)| name.clone())
        .collect::<Vec<_>>();
    let mut out = Vec::with_capacity(queue_count * interfaces.len());
    let mut slot = 0u32;
    for queue_id in 0..queue_count {
        for iface in &interfaces {
  ```

- **Trace:** 1. Interface A exposes four RX queues and interface B exposes two. 2. The planner selects global `queue_count = 2`, creates A/B sockets only for queues 0 and 1, and the Go publisher derives control `queue_count = 2`. 3. A receives a packet on hardware queue 2; this remains reachable on non-mlx5 devices, when RSS shaping is disabled/fails, when workers is 1, or when worker count differs from the global minimum. 4. `select_userspace_queue` returns `2 % 2 = 0`. 5. A's queue-0 binding is ready, so the fallback at lines 448-450 never looks for raw queue 2. 6. The shim returns `XDP_REDIRECT` to an XSK bound to A/queue 0 while the packet arrived on A/queue 2. The kernel's XSK-map queue check cannot deliver it and drops the packet. Every packet hashing to unbound raw queues can be blackholed persistently.

- **Refutation attempt:** The queue planner, control `queueCountFromBindings`, binding publisher, daemon RSS shaper, XSK binding status, and tests were inspected. RSS does not make the modulo safe: it is mlx5-only, explicitly best-effort, skipped for one worker, keyed to configured workers rather than the planner's per-interface minimum, and errors are swallowed. The raw-queue fallback is ineffective whenever the modulo-selected low queue exists, which is the normal planned state. `queue_planner_uses_smallest_queue_count` passes and confirms rather than refutes the trigger. No validator proves hardware traffic is restricted to the planned queue set.

- **HPC/invariant check:** AF_XDP's ownership invariant is `(netdev, actual RX queue) == socket binding`; modulo destroys that identity. The current operation is cheap but incorrect. Returning the raw queue removes modulo work; any replacement map must remain allocation-free and should be measured for lookup and instruction-cache cost.

- **Why it matters:** Enforcement remains fail-closed, but valid transit on higher hardware queues is silently dropped. On a mixed-queue router this can look like flow-dependent loss or throughput collapse and can survive indefinitely rather than only during reconcile.

- **Fix direction:** Never change the queue coordinate before XSK redirect. Publish/bind the actual queues for each interface and key lookup by full `(ifindex, rx_queue_index)`, or make exact RSS restriction to the published queue set a mandatory proven precondition that keeps control disabled on failure. Add an explicit `xdp_md` test for raw queues above the planner minimum and a real multi-queue AF_XDP integration test.

- **Labels:** `bug`, `availability`, `af-xdp`, `native-xdp-shim`

- **Dedup note:** No exact match was found. #805 concerns stale mlx5 RSS restoration and #1921 concerns virtio bind failure; this finding is the distinct global-minimum-plus-modulo violation even when all planned sockets are healthy.

  The frame contract confirms that cross-family NAT64 cannot be repaired by this in-place call (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/frame/mod.rs:229`):

  ```rust
  /// Build a forwarded frame for NAT64 packets. NAT64 changes the IP address
  /// family so the frame size changes (IPv6→IPv4 shrinks by 20, IPv4→IPv6 grows
  /// by 20). This always uses a copy path — in-place rewrite is not possible.
  pub(super) fn build_nat64_forwarded_frame(
      frame: &[u8],
      meta: impl Into<ForwardPacketMeta>,
      decision: &SessionDecision,
      nat64_reverse: Option<&Nat64ReverseInfo>,

- **Trace:** 1. An IPv6 packet targets a configured `/96` NAT64 prefix. 2. `classify_ipv6_dest` returns `MatchReady`, and route/neighbor lookup correctly uses the extracted IPv4 destination. 3. If that IPv4 next-hop MAC is absent, resolution is `MissingNeighbor` before the `ForwardCandidate` permit block that allocates the NAT64 source and calls `Nat64State::forward_decision`. 4. `decision.nat` therefore has no NAT64 flag or IPv4 rewrite; policy is evaluated on `flow.dst_ip`, the synthetic V6 address. 5. Under the legacy per-family convention, a permit scoped to an IPv4 destination has an empty V6 side that is `MatchAny`, so a real IPv4 destination outside that permit can be admitted only while the neighbor is unresolved. 6. The path installs a `MissingNeighborSeed` and buffers the UMEM frame with that incomplete decision. 7. On neighbor resolution, retry changes only the L2 MAC/disposition and calls the normal in-place rewrite; it neither classifies NAT64 nor allocates/restores the BIB. The original IPv6 packet can therefore be emitted toward the IPv4-selected next-hop MAC, and the installed state lacks the NAT64 reverse tuple.

- **Refutation attempt:** I inspected the primary NAT64 classifier/allocation, both policy sites, legacy/v3 per-family address semantics, session seed, pending-neighbor admission, retry rewrite, related tests, and git history for #2345, #2358, #4440/#4450, and #4449/#4460. #4440's “no bypass” conclusion is expressly limited to `ForwardCandidate`; #4460 confirms the MissingNeighbor divergence but changes only comments. The existing scoped test forces the branch and passes, but checks only `missing_neigh` and `policy_deny == 0`. There is no later reclassification in `retry_pending_neigh` and no guard that drops a NAT64-marked prefix before seeding. The claim therefore survives, with Medium rather than High severity because successful delivery of the malformed/untranslated packet depends on the upstream L2/L3 environment.

- **HPC/invariant check:** Descriptor ownership remains bounded to one buffered UMEM frame per next-hop key, and the retry slice is bounds-checked; this is not an unsafe/provenance defect. The broken invariants are fail-closed policy consistency (“neighbor cache state cannot change the policy tuple/verdict”), NAT state completeness (“a session routed as NAT64 must carry a NAT64 decision/BIB”), and packet-family consistency (“an IPv4 resolution target must not release the original IPv6 frame through same-family rewrite”). This is cold-path-only, but the incorrect session affects subsequent packets.

- **Why it matters:** Clearing or aging an ARP entry changes security-policy semantics for the same 5-tuple, can widen an IPv4-scoped permit through the opposite-family `MatchAny` convention, and creates state that cannot correctly reverse-translate replies. At minimum this blackholes NAT64 during neighbor discovery; in an environment where the selected WAN gateway also routes IPv6, it can leak the synthetic IPv6 packet upstream after an unintended permit.

- **Fix direction:** Either fail closed for NAT64 on `MissingNeighbor` and require a fresh packet after neighbor resolution, or carry/reconstruct `nat64_match` into that arm. The complete fix must evaluate policy on the extracted V4 destination, defer then perform unique source/port allocation after permit, store `Nat64State::forward_decision` plus `Nat64ReverseInfo`, install the correct cross-family reverse state, and roll allocation back on every seed/buffer failure. Add fail-on-revert tests with a nonmatching real V4 host, assertions on `pending_decision.nat.nat64` and BIB/reverse key, and a retry test that inspects emitted Ethertype/address family and translated bytes.

- **Labels:** `bug`, `security`, `afxdp`, `nat64`, `neighbor-resolution`, `fail-open`, `vsrx-parity`

- **Dedup note:** Distinct from #2358/PR #3273 and #4440/PR #4450, which address/verify only the resolved `ForwardCandidate` tuple. PR #4460 documents that this branch remains divergent but does not report or fix the incomplete seed/retry decision. No dedup-index entry covers the neighbor-state-dependent verdict plus non-NAT64 replay root cause.

### [A2-b1-F3] NPTv6 drops `from_zone`, so scoped static-NAT rules translate traffic from every zone

- **Title:** NPTv6 drops `from_zone`, so scoped static-NAT rules translate traffic from every zone

- **Severity:** Medium

- **Confidence:** High

- **Evidence:** The direct snapshot builder serializes the static rule-set scope (`pkg/dataplane/userspace/nat_nptv6.go:20-25`), but `userspace-dp/src/nptv6.rs:292-300` constructs a rule with no scope field:

```rust
            let rule = Nptv6Rule {
                internal_prefix,
                external_prefix,
                adjustment,
                prefix_words: iwords,
            };

            // Inbound: match external prefix on dst, rewrite to internal.
            state.inbound.push(rule.clone());
```

`Nptv6Rule` itself contains only prefixes, adjustment, and prefix length (`nptv6.rs:58-68`). Both lookup APIs accept only an address and select solely by prefix (`nptv6.rs:321-343`, `349-370`). Direct packet-path callers have ingress/egress zone context but cannot pass it (`afxdp/poll_descriptor/mod.rs:1590-1603`, `2804-2842`).

- **Trace:** 1. Configure an RFC 6296 rule under a static-NAT rule set scoped `from zone untrust`.
2. The Go snapshot carries `from_zone="untrust"`.
3. `try_from_snapshots` discards that value and publishes global inbound/outbound prefix vectors.
4. A packet entering from `dmz` (or another tenant zone) for the external prefix still receives inbound destination translation; an internal-prefix source leaving toward a zone other than `untrust` still receives outbound source translation.
5. Rules that legitimately reuse the same prefixes in distinct zones cannot express split-horizon behavior either: the global overlap check rejects them as overlapping before scope could separate them.

- **Refutation attempt:** I checked whether `from_zone` was informational or enforced at a caller. The wire struct and builder deliberately carry it, sibling static NAT uses `from` scope in both directions, and no NPTv6 caller performs a zone guard before invoking the address-only API. The `real_world_prefixes` test sets `from_zone="untrust"` but then translates without zone context, which demonstrates the omission rather than refuting it. No dedup entry covers NPTv6 zone scope.

- **HPC/invariant check:** The intended invariant is that an NPTv6 rule may match only in its static-NAT rule-set scope (inbound ingress zone and reverse/outbound egress zone). Current translation is allocation-free and lock-free; storing a compact zone identifier/string and comparing it during the existing linear prefix scan preserves those properties. Overlap validation must be partitioned by mutually exclusive scope.

- **Why it matters:** Prefix ownership often overlaps across VRFs/tenants/zones. Globalizing a scoped rule can translate and route traffic into the wrong security domain, or rewrite internal sources on paths where no NPTv6 mapping was intended.

- **Fix direction:** Preserve `from_zone` in `Nptv6Rule`; pass ingress zone to inbound translation and egress zone to outbound/reverse translation; treat empty scope as wildcard. Partition overlap rejection by scope and add wrong-zone, correct-zone, reverse-direction, and same-prefix split-horizon tests.

- **Labels:** userspace-dp, nptv6, static-nat, security, vsrx-parity

- **Dedup note:** #2241 addressed ambiguous overlapping prefixes in the existing global table; #2380 addressed NPTv6 host bits. Neither addressed the discarded rule-set scope. Scope-aware overlap validation is a consequence of this distinct root cause.

### [A2-b1-F4] NAT64 ICMP errors restore embedded addresses but leave the translated PAT port/identifier in the quoted packet

- **Title:** NAT64 ICMP errors restore embedded addresses but leave the translated PAT port/identifier in the quoted packet

- **Severity:** Medium

- **Confidence:** High

- **Evidence:** `userspace-dp/src/nat64.rs:2487-2492` maps the embedded IPv4 addresses back to the IPv6 endpoints and then copies the quoted L4 bytes verbatim:

```rust
    // Embedded src (our SNAT pool v4) -> original v6 client.
    out[8..24].copy_from_slice(&map.mapped_embedded_src.octets());
    // Embedded dst (the v4 server) -> NAT64 prefix :: dst-v4.
    out[24..36].copy_from_slice(&map.prefix_bytes);
    out[36..40].copy_from_slice(&quote_in[16..20]);
    out[40..total].copy_from_slice(l4);
```

The regression test explicitly requires preservation of the translated quote at `userspace-dp/src/nat64_tests.rs:1921-1928`. After #4381, however, the embedded source TCP/UDP port or ICMP query identifier is normally a newly allocated value. The direct AF_XDP caller rewrites only the outer L4 header after family translation (`afxdp/frame/mod.rs:319-330`); for an ICMP error that helper does not descend into the quote.

- **Trace:** 1. An IPv6 TCP client opens from source port 12345; NAT64 allocates public `198.51.100.1:40000` and sends that tuple to the IPv4 server.
2. A server/router returns ICMPv4 unreachable, time-exceeded, or fragmentation-needed quoting `198.51.100.1:40000 -> server:port`.
3. Reverse NAT64 maps the quoted source address to the original IPv6 client and the destination to the synthetic server address, but copies source port 40000 unchanged.
4. The frame-level NAT decision carries the original port, but the outer packet is an ICMPv6 error, not a TCP/UDP/echo query, so the normal outer port/identifier rewrite is a no-op.
5. The IPv6 host receives an internally inconsistent quote (`client-v6:40000`, not `client-v6:12345`). TCP/UDP/ICMP socket lookup cannot reliably associate the error with the originating flow; asynchronous errors, traceroute attribution, and per-flow PMTUD can be lost.

- **Refutation attempt:** I inspected both embedded translators, outer ICMP finalization, frame-level port rewrite, tests, and the #2371 history. The outer checksum is recomputed correctly after the quote is copied, but checksum correctness does not restore the original tuple. #2371 fixed embedded transport checksum adjustment, not BIB/PAT port reversal. No later helper parses or rewrites the embedded quote, and the current test fixture uses the same bytes as the expected output.

- **HPC/invariant check:** For an ICMP error delivered to the inside host, the embedded invoking tuple must equal the tuple that host emitted, including the pre-PAT source port/query identifier. The quote is already bounded (`MAX_EMBEDDED_LEN`) and copied on the ICMP slow path. Rewriting the first transport field from session NAT metadata adds no packet-path allocation; outer ICMP checksum finalization must include the changed quote. Embedded L4 checksums remain informational but should be adjusted when enough bytes are present, consistent with #2371.

- **Why it matters:** Data forwarding can appear healthy while control/error traffic is detached from the socket that needs it. The operational result is stalled large transfers, ignored unreachable errors, or misleading traceroute behavior after stateful NAT64 PAT.

- **Fix direction:** Pass the forward/reverse `NatDecision` (or explicit original/translated L4 values) into embedded translation. For reverse v4-to-v6 errors, rewrite the quoted source port/ICMP identifier to the original client value; implement the symmetric direction where applicable. Recompute the outer ICMP checksum after the quote update and add fixtures where original and translated ports/identifiers differ.

- **Labels:** userspace-dp, nat64, icmp, checksum, pmtud

- **Dedup note:** #2371 is limited to embedded checksum correctness, and #4381 is limited to allocating/applying unique outer ports. This is the unhandled composition of those features: reversing the stateful port mapping inside an ICMP quote. No matching dedup entry was found.

### [A2-b1-F5] Synced deterministic NAT reservations are released into a recycle queue that deterministic allocation never drains

- **Title:** Synced deterministic NAT reservations are released into a recycle queue that deterministic allocation never drains

- **Severity:** Medium

- **Confidence:** High

- **Evidence:** `userspace-dp/src/nat/allocator.rs:1515-1523` records every exact HA reservation as non-deterministic:

```rust
        live.live_by_flow.insert(
            flow,
            LiveAllocation {
                translated,
                persistent_key: None,
                addr_index,
                deterministic: false,
            },
        );
```

`allocator.rs:1231-1240` therefore recycles it on release:

```rust
        } else {
            // Non-persistent (or deterministic) flow owns its port outright:
            // free the bit, recycling it unless it is a deterministic block
            // port (#4559). The persistent case keeps the port on the lease
            // until the lease itself is torn down.
            self.free_translated_port(
                existing.addr_index,
                translated.port,
                !existing.deterministic,
            );
```

The recycle operation unconditionally `push_back`s with no cap/dedup (`allocator.rs:556-569`), while the deterministic path explicitly never drains the queue (`allocator.rs:572-579`, `1305-1316`, `1384-1394`). Both source NAT and NAT64 sync wrappers call `reserve_flow` without deterministic mode (`source.rs:803-851`, `nat64.rs:1097-1128`).

- **Trace:** 1. On a standby with deterministic CGNAT/NAPT64 configured, a peer session upsert reserves its exact translated block port via `reserve_flow`.
2. The record is tagged `deterministic=false`, even though the local rule/prefix is deterministic.
3. Peer delete, reap, purge, or rollback reaches the normal `release_flow`; it clears the bit and pushes the port onto the per-address FIFO recycle queue.
4. Deterministic allocation scans the subscriber block and uses `reserve(port)` directly; it never consumes the FIFO. Sequential sessions can repeatedly reuse and then re-enqueue the same low block port, creating duplicate stale entries.
5. The allocator Arc survives compatible reloads, so queue memory grows with deterministic HA session churn until helper restart or a mode change that happens to consume it.

- **Refutation attempt:** Local deterministic allocation sets `LiveAllocation.deterministic=true`, and its tests prove release avoids recycle. The synced-session tests use ordinary round-robin pools and therefore do not exercise the missing mode. `max_tracked_flows` caps simultaneously live map entries, not the `VecDeque`, and `free_recycle` has no capacity or membership guard. Stable deterministic operation provides no consumer, so the resource leak survives.

- **HPC/invariant check:** A deterministic block port's occupancy bit is its only reuse gate; its lifetime must never create recycle metadata. Current atomic bit ownership remains correct, but every teardown takes the per-address recycle mutex and may allocate/grow `VecDeque`, creating unbounded control-path memory and cache work. The invariant should be encoded in exact reservations, not inferred at release time from a rule that may have changed.

- **Why it matters:** CGNAT HA deployments have high session churn. Linear, unbounded standby memory growth can eventually cause allocator latency, helper memory pressure, or process failure even though live-flow and used-port status remain low.

- **Fix direction:** Extend `reserve_flow` with allocation mode/provenance and set `deterministic=true` when the owning source rule or NAT64 prefix is deterministic. Alternatively add a no-recycle exact reservation API. Bound/deduplicate recycle queues defensively, expose queue depth, and add repeated deterministic sync upsert/delete tests for source NAT and NAT64 across compatible reloads.

- **Labels:** userspace-dp, nat, cgnat, nat64, ha, resource-lifetime

- **Dedup note:** #4388/#4512 fixed the absence of standby port reservations and their collision consequence. This is a materially different post-fix lifecycle bug: reservation succeeds, but teardown loses deterministic provenance and accumulates unconsumed recycle state.

The map lookup sets `isSet=true`, so `ExpandApplicationSet` runs. 4. `lookupApplicationSet` returns `(nil, true)` because the key exists. 5. The `!ok` error guard is bypassed and `as.Applications` dereferences nil. 6. `BuildCatalog`/snapshot construction cannot return an error and retain the previous-good dataplane state; the panic terminates the calling control-plane process/goroutine path.

The claim survives.

The critical invariant is error-returned partial failure: malformed tolerant input must either be skipped honestly or return an error so the previous/default-deny snapshot remains active. A panic bypasses that transaction boundary. The recursion cap and allocation bounds do not protect the nil dereference.

- **Why it matters:** A malformed but intentionally tolerated null slot can turn policy/NAT reference collection into a repeatable control-plane crash during load, sync, or snapshot/apply. That defeats the no-brick posture and removes the opportunity to fail closed with the prior snapshot.

- **Fix direction:** Make `lookupApplicationSet`/`ExpandApplicationSet` distinguish a present nil value and return a deterministic error, or nil-check in `CatalogNames` before expansion. Propagate the error through `BuildCatalog` so apply retains prior state. Add direct-reference and nested-reference tests for nil application-set values on strict, lenient, and catalog paths.

- **Labels:** `pkg-appid`, `panic`, `tolerant-load`, `ha-sync`, `fail-closed`

On a strict commit, current validators reject a referenced/all-catalog app with missing or unknown protocol, and reject a bare source/destination port `0`; on lenient load those errors are warnings and the typed values remain. 2. With application-identification enabled, `CatalogNames` includes even an unreferenced malformed user app, so no policy-content rejection is needed to reach catalog construction. 3. Suppress both row and name (while preserving the agreed ID-consumption rule) or return a fail-closed catalog error, and mirror the decision in `compileApplications`. Add lenient tests for unknown protocol, missing protocol, bare source/destination zero, and `0-0`.

171         as := &ApplicationSet{Name: inst.name}
172
173         for _, member := range inst.node.Children {
174             // An application-set member is either an individual application
175             // reference (`application <name>`) or a nested application-set
176             // reference (`application-set <name>`). Both kinds are stored in
177             // as.Applications; ExpandApplicationSet distinguishes them by
178             // looking each member name up in apps.ApplicationSets and recursing
```

The member arm at `pkg/config/compiler_applications.go:183` appends only scalar `nodeVal`:

```go
183             switch member.Name() {
184             case "application", "application-set":
185                 v := nodeVal(member)
186                 if v != "" {
187                     as.Applications = append(as.Applications, v)
188                 }
```

`nodeVal` explicitly selects only `Keys[1]` or the first child at `pkg/config/compiler_applications.go:724`:

```go
724 func nodeVal(n *Node) string {
725     if len(n.Keys) >= 2 {
726         return n.Keys[1]
727     }
728     if len(n.Children) > 0 {
729         return n.Children[0].Name()
730     }
731     return ""
```

- **Trace:** 1. `application-set blocked { application [ app1 app2 ]; }` produces one member node with `Keys=["application","app1","app2"]`. 2. The compiler enters the member once. 3. `nodeVal` returns `app1`; `app2` is discarded. 4. The resulting set is nonempty and all retained references resolve, so strict syntax/reference/empty-set gates pass. 5. A deny policy matching `blocked` expands only `app1`. 6. Traffic matching defined `app2` falls through to a later policy/default rather than the authored deny.

None retain or validate the raw member cardinality after `nodeVal` truncates it. Existing valid-member tests use separate nodes.

- **HPC/invariant check:** Local slice ownership and bounded set recursion are sound; there is no concurrency. The violated invariant is that list-valued leaves must consume `Keys[1:]` and child values identically across AST shapes. Runtime matching remains fast but receives an incomplete set.

- **Why it matters:** A syntactically valid Junos application set can under-populate a deny rule with no warning, creating a policy fail-open and vSRX migration mismatch.

- **Fix direction:** Use a shared full-value extractor for both `application` and `application-set` member nodes, preserve ordering/dedup rules, and add hierarchical and flat bracket-list tests that assert all direct and nested members reach policy expansion.

- **Labels:** `config`, `security`, `fail-open`, `dual-ast`, `vsrx-parity`

60                 if n, err := strconv.Atoi(v); err == nil {

`pkg/config/compiler_ipsec_proposalset.go:112` generates a predictable name using characters the lexer also permits in operator names:

```go

113 // for a proposal synthesized from a policy's proposal-set. The rendered
114 // swanctl proposal is the crypto token string (buildIKEProposalFromIKE /
115 // buildESPProposal), not this name, so the name is internal only; the "__"
116 // prefix and slashes keep it clear of operator-authored proposal names.
117 func syntheticProposalSetName(policy, set string, n int) string {
118     return fmt.Sprintf("__proposal-set/%s/%s/%d", policy, set, n)
119 }
```

Expansion unconditionally overwrites the same map at `pkg/config/compiler_ipsec_proposalset.go:144`:

```go
144         for i, s := range specs {
145             name := syntheticProposalSetName(pol.Name, pol.ProposalSet, i+1)
146             sec.IPsec.IKEProposals[name] = &IKEProposal{
147                 Name:          name,
148                 AuthMethod:    s.authMethod,
149                 EncryptionAlg: s.enc,
150                 AuthAlg:       s.auth,
151                 DHGroup:       s.dhGroup,
152             }
153             pol.Proposals = append(pol.Proposals, name)

The directly called lexer contract at `pkg/config/lexer.go:289` confirms `/` and `_` are valid bare identifier characters:

```go
289 func isIdentChar(ch byte) bool {
290     return (ch >= 'a' && ch <= 'z') ||
291         (ch >= 'A' && ch <= 'Z') ||
292         (ch >= '0' && ch <= '9') ||
293         ch == '-' || ch == '_' || ch == '.' ||
294         ch == '/' || ch == ':' || ch == '*' || ch == '+' ||
295         ch == '%' || ch == '=' || ch == ',' ||
296         ch == '<' || ch == '>'
```

- **Trace:** 1. An operator defines proposal `__proposal-set/P/standard/1` with strong crypto and has policy `Q` reference it. 2. Policy `P` selects `proposal-set standard`. 3. `compileIKE` stores the authored proposal and both policies. 4. `expandIKEProposalSets` generates the same predictable name and overwrites the authored map entry. 5. Reference validation sees a defined, structurally valid proposal, so commit succeeds. 6. Policy `Q` negotiates the generated legacy `standard` member rather than its authored crypto. The phase-2 mirror has the same behavior in `sec.IPsec.Proposals`.

No reserved-prefix rejection or collision check exists for either proposal map. The comment's assumption that slash keeps names internal is false under the lexer contract.

- **HPC/invariant check:** Fixed-size proposal sets make CPU/memory bounded; no concurrency or secret lifetime issue. The violated invariant is namespace ownership: generated internal identities must be unrepresentable by users or collision-checked before map insertion.

- **Why it matters:** A valid imported/operator proposal can silently change cipher/auth/DH selection for another policy, including downgrade to the legacy `standard/basic/compatible` suites, while validation and rendered references remain internally consistent.

- **Fix direction:** Reserve and strictly reject the synthetic prefix for authored IKE/IPsec proposal names, or keep generated proposals in a separate typed namespace. - **Labels:** `config`, `ipsec`, `crypto`, `name-collision`, `vsrx-parity`

- **Dedup note:** Distinct from `#4297`, which implemented proposal-set expansion. This finding is a generated/operator namespace collision introduced by that expansion; the prior issue did not cover authored proposals named like synthetic members.

Parse hierarchical `security screen ids-option edge { tcp { land; } tcp { syn-fin; } }`. 2. `parseStatements` appends both `tcp` nodes without a parse error. 3. `compileScreen` calls `inst.node.FindChild("tcp")`; the contract returns the first sibling only. 4. `land` enters the compiled `ScreenProfile`, while `syn-fin` is never visited or recorded as unknown. 5. Strict screen validators iterate the already-compiled `cfg.Security.Screen` map, see a valid profile, and return success. 6. The zone references that profile and the dataplane receives no `syn-fin` protection. Repeated same-name `ids-option` blocks have a second loss mode: each creates a fresh profile and `sec.Screen[profile.Name] = profile` at `compiler_security_screen.go:471` replaces the earlier one.

- **Refutation attempt:** I inspected parser sibling retention, `FindChild` semantics, all screen strict validators, top-level security dispatch, dual-AST fixtures, and screen-specific tests. Numeric and unknown-leaf gates cannot help because the omitted sibling never reaches `BadNumeric` or `UnknownLeaves`; the reference gate only verifies the profile name exists. The differential screen fixture contains one block per family, and no duplicate-screen test refutes the trace.

- **HPC/invariant check:** No unsafe code, aliasing, atomics, locks, descriptor ownership, or release-profile branch issue is involved. Compilation is linear, and the dataplane consumes immutable booleans. The violated invariant is stronger: every valid hierarchical sibling must contribute to the same compiled profile, and hierarchical and flat-set ASTs must compile equivalently.

- **Why it matters:** A commit succeeds while an explicitly configured screen defense is absent. This is fail-open security behavior and a Junos/vSRX merge-semantics parity gap, not merely a diagnostic discrepancy.

- **Fix direction:** Iterate `FindChildren` for each repeatable family and merge every subtree into one profile; merge repeated same-name `ids-option` instances instead of replacing the map value. Add differential tests with repeated `tcp`, `icmp`, and same-name profile blocks, asserting strict and lenient output equality with equivalent flat-set commands.

- **Labels:** `config`, `security`, `parser`, `dual-ast`, `fail-open`, `vsrx-parity`

- **Dedup note:** Distinct from closed #3566. That issue was first-child traversal in raw-AST flow/log validators; here the screen compiler loses valid state before compiled-state validators run. No screen duplicate/compiler-truncation root appears in the dedup index.

     252			}
     253		}

     248            // learned endpoint (#1736).

     252                .ok()
     253                .map(crate::afxdp::wg::canonicalize_endpoint);

- **Trace:** 1. Author the standard IPv6 peer endpoint `[2001:db8::10]:51820`. 2. The existing tokenizer/compiler path stores only bare `2001:db8::10`; comments at `compiler_validate_wireguard.go:240-245` and `types_routing.go:593-595` document that behavior. 3. `endpointIsV6` accepts that bare IP and the family gate succeeds. 4. The snapshot carries the same non-empty bare IP. 5. Rust `parse::<SocketAddr>()` fails because there is no port, `.ok()` turns the error into `None`, and hydration keeps the peer. 6. `None` means responder-only: proactive handshakes and persistent keepalives cannot target the configured endpoint.

- **Refutation attempt:** I inspected the WireGuard schema, `parseTunnelWireguardPeer`, the strict peer validator, outer-family derivation, tunnel snapshot fields, Rust hydration, and relevant Go/Rust tests. No stage reattaches the stripped port or rejects a non-empty endpoint that hydrates to `None`. Existing mixed-family tests establish family classification but do not assert the end-to-end runtime `SocketAddr` for bracketed IPv6.

Hydration is cold and bounded. The violated invariant is that every non-empty endpoint accepted at strict commit must hydrate to `Some(SocketAddr)` with the authored port.

- **Severity:** Medium

- **Confidence:** High

  ```go

     171					}

     173						warnings = append(warnings, fmt.Sprintf(

     175								"overlapping L3 across routing-instances is forwarded via "+
     176								"PBR but is NOT session-isolated (#2387) — colliding "+
